Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Relationship Reminders: When people say things like my ex
issues.explanation: This trigger is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. For a 21-year-old married male relief worker in a war zone, military topics and Arabic shouting fit the reported trauma context, but 'my ex' is relationship-specific and not plausibly linked to the war-zone trauma as presented. It also does not connect well to the accompanying threat and memory items, which are clearly organized around combat/civilian danger cues rather than intimate-relationship themes.

vignette: Alex is twenty-one, a recent college graduate who has married his high school sweetheart, Mara, after a brief engagement. He works as a social ministry worker at a downtown community center that hosts weekly support groups for veterans. The center's bright, airy hall is filled with laughter and music most days, yet the hum of voices sometimes carries the sharp intonation of distant war talk that Alex can't ignore. The memory of his last assignment as a relief worker in Aleppo, where he had to move through rubble and watch civilians drown in fear, lingers in him as a vivid, unfiltered echo. The first time Alex hears a colleague bring up military topics-a drone strike last week-he feels a surge of unease that forces him to postpone bedtime. He lies awake, eyes staring at the ceiling, thinking how he could have prevented the collapse of that makeshift shelter. The same rush follows each time the building's PA system crackles with Arabic shouting from the neighboring mosque. These auditory intrusions have become triggers that push Alex into a defensive posture: he delays sleep, ruminates on the impossibility of averting the tragedy, and deliberately stays away from any event that might stir joy, fearing it will open a doorway to the terror he can't let go of. When Alex listens to the military vocabulary of a new volunteer, his sense of personal safety frays. He feels the sudden, phantom presence of strangers lurking in the shadows, as if every passing passer-by could become a threat. This heightened threat perception becomes almost automatic: he watches the crowd for any sudden movement, his eyes flicking to the doorways, to the brief pause before someone enters. Even in the normal rhythm of the community center, strangers' footsteps echo with danger in his mind, amplifying his alertness and causing him to scan the room for any hint of imminent harm. The memory of the Aleppo explosion surfaces in Alex each time a trigger lands. He hears the metallic clatter of artillery and finds himself suddenly reliving the image of the shattered doorway, the screams of children, the cold shock that set his heart to pounding. The vividness of this recollection feels almost tangible, as if the scene were unfolding in front of him again. His mind can't distinguish between the past event and the present moment; the terror that once surged at the blast returns with each recall. Because this intrusive memory replays with such intensity, Alex's coping mechanisms become more entrenched. The urge to stay awake through the night intensifies his rumination: he spends hours mentally retracing the steps he could have taken to avert the collapse of that shelter. He consciously steers clear of the community center's Friday potluck, an event that once promised laughter and shared meals, because the thought of being surrounded by smiling faces feels like a trap waiting to unleash the same panic. The memory itself keeps feeding Alex's sense of danger. Every time he recalls the explosion, the brain's threat-detection system is triggered, and he feels compelled to scan his environment, to check whether the people around him are a threat. He wakes during the night to look through the blinds for intruders, to hear the faintest creak of the hallway, and then, as if in a loop, he wakes again to the memory's call. Alex's perception of threat also fuels his own triggers. Knowing that even a stranger's approach can spark a flashback, he deliberately avoids the community center's busy street corner where a bus stop is located. He chooses instead to stay home, to keep his phone away, to keep the door locked, thereby reducing the opportunities for the triggers to surface and to keep the cycle of threat perception and memory intrusion tight. The maladaptive strategies Alex has adopted-sleep deprivation, rumination, and avoidance-reinforce the memories he struggles to suppress. His exhausted state amplifies the vividness of his recollections: the images sharpen, the emotions become more overwhelming, and the fear that once was in the past now feels like a living, breathing presence that he can't escape. The sleepless nights leave him more exhausted, more irritable, and more prone to misinterpret normal events as hostile. For months, Alex's avoidance has cost him professional progress and personal joy. He has missed several church events, he has turned down invitations from Mara to celebrate their anniversary, and his supervisor has noted a decline in his engagement with the volunteer team. He now recognizes that the cycle is tightening-every trigger, every memory, every threat perception feeding back into each other in a relentless loop. The fear that once felt like a distant echo has become a constant, a storm that clouds his everyday life. It is this realization-this dawning awareness that his avoidance has not spared him from the trauma but rather fed it-that finally drives Alex to seek help, hoping to break the chain and reclaim the sense of safety and hope he once took for granted.
